slides: Now team questions. They're also called worker questions.

slides.say: They're considered hard. Not because of the arithmetic, but because they need real understanding. With one table and one method, they become quick.
In the last lesson, each worker had a different rate. Here, every worker has the same rate.
How do we spot a team question? First, the words identical, and constant rate.
So the workers are like robots. They all work at the same speed, and they never get tired.
Second, a group of workers. Usually more than two, like five painters or eight machines.
When we see both, it's a team question.
In a team, every worker adds the same rate. Let's see it in numbers.
One worker packs four boxes an hour.
So five identical workers pack five times four, twenty boxes an hour.
So the team's rate is the number of workers, times one worker's rate.
That's why the team size matters. Twice the workers do twice the work in the same time.
at: Twice the workers do twice the work

slides.say: Or they do the same work in half the time. Like in the first lesson, the work is fixed, so the team and the time go opposite ways.
at: the same work in half the time

slides.say: Every team question goes into a table with three columns, team, work and time.

slides: The work always sits in the middle. How do we remember the order? Teamwork takes time. Team, work, time.
Row one is what they give us. Row two is what they ask about.

slides.say: Here's an example. Six cooks make thirty pies in two hours. How many hours do four cooks need for forty pies?
Row one is six cooks, thirty pies and two hours.
Row two is four cooks and forty pies. The question mark goes in the time.
The first way is ratios. We look at each change, and ask what it does to the time. We want the time, so we start from the two hours.
The pies go from thirty to forty. That's times four thirds. More work takes more time, the same way. So the time is times four thirds too.
at: time is times four thirds too

slides.say: The cooks go from six to four. That's times two thirds. Fewer cooks take more time. That's the opposite way, so we flip it. The time is times three halves.
at: The time is times three halves

slides.say: So the time is two, times four thirds, times three halves.
at: So the time is two, times

slides.say: Four thirds times three halves. The threes cancel, and four over two is two. So two times two is four hours.
at: So two times two is four

slides.say: Like in the first lesson. The same way, we multiply as it is. The opposite way, we flip it. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
